Neonatal North Atlantic right whales are among the largest mammalian newborns, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 794,328 grams [Wwb = approximately 794,328 grams]. This substantial initial mass reflects the intense maternal investment characteristic of balaenopterids and provides a crucial energetic buffer during the first weeks of life. Weaning occurs relatively early for such a large mammal; the average time since birth at weaning is 213 days [tx = 213 days], a duration that corresponds to the period when the calf transitions from exclusive milk dependence to the onset of filter-feeding on copepods. at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]During this early nursing phase, which takes place within the species' typical core body temperature range of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the calf grows rapidly, relying on its mother's lipid-rich milk to accumulate the blubber reserves necessary for thermoregulation in the cold North Atlantic waters. Field observations indicate that this weaning interval, while brief relative to lifespan, is nonetheless a critical bottleneck in calf survival, as the nutritional independence is acquired before the calf has fully mastered the foraging techniques used by adults.

Gestation in Eubalaena glacialis lasts approximately 350 days [tg = approximately 350 days], a duration measured under the thermal conditions of a healthy adult female's core temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This relatively long gestation period, comparable to that of other large cetaceans, is tied to the extensive foetal growth required to produce a calf weighing over three-quarters of a tonne. Following parturition, the newborn begins suckling almost immediately, initiating a period of intense maternal care. The long gestation and subsequent lactation place a substantial energetic burden on the mother, who typically cannot breed again for another year or more. Recent photogrammetric studies have linked prolonged gestation to the need for the foetus to attain a critical body size before birth, which is hypothesized to enhance neonatal survival in the thermally demanding environment of the species' calving grounds off the southeastern United States. This protracted prenatal development underscores the life-history strategy of a species that prioritizes high per-offspring investment over high fecundity.

Under the stable thermal conditions maintained by the species' physiological thermoregulation at 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the maximum voluntary reproductive rate is exceptionally low. Long-term photographic databases reveal that, on average, a mature female produces one calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = one calf per reproductive event], occurring on average every 3.3 years [F_R_i = occurring on average every 3.3 years]. This translates to one of the slowest reproductive rates of any cetacean, a consequence of the combination of a lengthy gestation, a multi-year lactation period, and the high energetic costs of supporting a large calf. The interval between successive calving events can extend further following unsuccessful pregnancies or in years of poor prey abundance, especially when the copepod Calanus finmarchicus is scarce in the primary foraging grounds. This intrinsic constraint on population growth is a critical factor in the species' vulnerability to anthropogenic mortality, as even a small increase in deaths can outpace the replacement capacity of the population.

The time since birth at puberty for this species is estimated at 2,920 days [tp = 2,920 days] when measured at the typical adult body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This exceptionally delayed onset of sexual maturity, lasting roughly eight years, sets right whales apart from smaller delphinids and is characteristic of the extremely slow life-history pace of mysticetes. During this protracted juvenile and sub-adult period, individuals allocate almost all ingested energy toward somatic growth rather than reproductive development, gradually building the massive body frame necessary to support a large foetus and to store the energetic reserves needed for successful reproduction. Puberty itself is not immediately followed by successful breeding; first-time mothers often experience higher rates of calf mortality, suggesting that the attainment of sexual maturity does not guarantee reproductive competence. The extended prepubertal phase is thus an adaptive strategy that trades early reproduction for high per-capita offspring survival in a seasonally variable ocean environment.

Maximum recorded longevity for the North Atlantic right whale, observed in photo-identification studies spanning multiple decades, is 67 years [am = 67 years] under their normal body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This lifespan, while impressive, is considerably shorter than that of the bowhead whale, a closely related balaenid that can live over two centuries. The adult body mass in this species is similarly immense; the ultimate wet weight attained by large, healthy individuals reaches 23,000,000 grams [Wwi = 23,000,000 grams]. This enormous mass, coupled with a slow maturation rate and low fecundity, creates a population dynamic that is exceptionally sensitive to external disturbances. The contrast between a 23-tonne adult and a 794-kilogram calf highlights the impressive growth trajectory that must be completed over roughly a decade. The documented lifespan is now under threat from chronic entanglement and vessel strike injuries, which have compressed the average reproductive lifespan of females and reduced the number of calves produced over an individual's lifetime.
